messages.content: I want to investigate embodied grounding of action verbs in a way that transfers across robot morphologies. The key distinction is between an action’s intended effect and the motion a robot happens to make. How should I state the goal?

The goal is to ground action verbs in what an instruction is meant to accomplish, without treating a particular observed motion as the definition of the verb. That grounding should transfer to robot morphologies the system has not seen before, even when their movements look different from those of familiar robots.
I also want the success requirement to remain explicit, not just an aspiration to transfer.

The stated target is ≥70% instruction success on unseen morphologies when motion cues conflict with intended effects. That is a target under a specific condition: the movements provide cues that do not straightforwardly agree with what the instruction is intended to achieve. It is not a claim that the target has already been reached.
Why emphasize the conflict between motion cues and intended effects?

Because agreement between them can obscure what the system is relying on. If a familiar-looking movement and the intended effect point in the same direction, successful behavior alone may not reveal whether the verb was grounded in the effect or merely associated with that movement. The conflict condition makes the distinction central to the goal.
So motion is not irrelevant; it just cannot be the whole meaning of the verb?

Exactly. Observed motion can be useful evidence about what is happening. The goal does not require ignoring it. It requires distinguishing that evidence from the intended effect, so a motion cue does not override the effect the instruction calls for when the two conflict.
There are two comparisons I especially care about: identical motions with different effects, and different motions with the same instructed effect.

Both are part of the requirement. The system should distinguish cases in which identical motions produce different effects, rather than treating the shared motion as proof that the action has the same meaning in each case. It should also recognize when different motions achieve the same instructed effect, rather than rejecting one solely because it looks unlike another.
Can you unpack the first comparison without assuming a particular robot or experiment?

At the conceptual level, imagine observing the same motion on two occasions, but the resulting effects differ. A motion-only interpretation would be tempted to classify the occasions alike. The requested distinction is to notice that the effects differ, despite the identical motions. That illustration does not specify what produced the difference or prescribe how to detect it.
And the converse comparison?

Two robots may move differently while achieving the same effect specified by an instruction. The system should be able to recognize that common achievement despite the difference in motion. This matters for transfer across robot morphologies: different bodies need not express an instructed action through the same movement.
Does saying “intended effect” imply that the effect actually occurred?

No. The intended effect is what the instruction calls for; the observed effect is what happens. Keeping those distinct is important when judging instruction success. A movement can suggest an attempt at an action without establishing that the intended effect was achieved.
Then the two comparisons concern outcomes, not just how an action looks?

Yes. For identical motions, the requirement is to distinguish the different effects they produce. For different motions, it is to recognize when they achieve the same instructed effect. In both comparisons, appearance of movement alone is insufficient to settle whether the relevant effect was achieved.
How narrowly should I read “unseen morphologies” in the success target?

It means the ≥70% instruction-success target applies to robot morphologies the system has not seen before. The goal does not specify particular body designs or a particular way to represent them. Its point is that grounding in an instructed effect should not depend on having encountered the same form of robot or the same-looking movement.
I do not want the target accidentally restated as 70% on ordinary instructions.

Then retain the full condition whenever you state it: ≥70% instruction success on unseen morphologies when motion cues conflict with intended effects. Omitting either unseen morphologies or the conflict condition would broaden the claim beyond the stated requirement.
Could someone satisfy the two motion-and-effect comparisons but still miss the numerical target?

The comparisons and the threshold express different parts of the goal. The comparisons describe distinctions the grounding should make; the ≥70% target specifies instruction success under the stated unseen-morphology, conflicting-cue condition. The node does not say that demonstrating one part automatically establishes the other.
Would it be accurate to say this is about action verbs across bodies, rather than one canonical way to move?

Yes. That phrasing captures the transfer aim. An action verb should remain connected to the effect an instruction intends even when a robot with a different morphology moves differently. At the same time, a familiar or identical motion should not erase a difference in the effects produced.
I want to avoid suggesting that every different-looking movement counts as the same action.

The requirement is more specific than that. Different motions should be recognized as equivalent in the relevant sense when they achieve the same instructed effect. If they do not achieve that effect, difference in morphology or movement does not by itself make the instruction successful.
Likewise, identical movement should not automatically mean a different action every time the outcome changes, should it?

The requirement is to distinguish the different effects, not to impose a universal label for every case of identical motion. It asks the grounding to preserve the effect-level difference that a purely motion-based reading would miss, while leaving unspecified any broader naming scheme.
Can we put the whole objective in one compact statement while keeping both comparisons and the threshold?

Investigate embodied grounding of action verbs that transfers across robot morphologies by distinguishing intended effects from observed motions: target ≥70% instruction success on unseen morphologies when motion cues conflict with intended effects, distinguish identical motions that produce different effects, and recognize different motions that achieve the same instructed effect.
That still reads as an investigation with a target, not as a completed result?

Yes. “Investigate” identifies the work, and “target” identifies the required level of success. Neither says that ≥70% instruction success has already been achieved or that either motion-and-effect distinction has already been demonstrated.
What is the central mistake this goal is trying to avoid?

It is the mistake of equating an action verb with one observed motion pattern. That would make identical motions seem equivalent even when they produce different effects, and different motions seem unrelated even when they achieve the same instructed effect. The goal instead keeps motion and intended effect distinct while testing whether that distinction transfers to unseen morphologies.
So the success criterion and those two comparisons should stay together when discussing the goal?

They belong to the same goal, but each retains its own meaning. The ≥70% criterion concerns instruction success on unseen morphologies specifically when motion cues conflict with intended effects. The paired comparisons spell out the effect-sensitive understanding sought: tell apart the effects of identical motions, and recognize a shared instructed effect across different motions.
What training proposal would directly address the distinction between observed motion and intended effect?

Train EffectBind using contrastive rollouts of two kinds: same-motion/different-effect rollouts, and cross-morphology different-motion/same-effect rollouts. The aim is to learn morphology-invariant verb embeddings for goal-conditioned control. This is a proposed approach, not a claim that EffectBind has already learned those embeddings.
Why use both kinds of rollout rather than just showing different robots achieving the same effect?

They address complementary confusions. Cross-morphology different-motion/same-effect rollouts emphasize that different movements can achieve the same effect. Same-motion/different-effect rollouts emphasize that matching movements do not guarantee matching effects. Together, they make motion alone an unreliable shortcut for grounding the verb.
What does “contrastive” mean in this proposal?

It means the training examples are arranged around meaningful similarities and differences. Here, a shared effect despite different motions is a similarity the representation should capture; a different effect despite the same motion is a difference it should preserve. The proposal does not specify a particular contrastive loss or training procedure beyond that idea.
Does the first kind of rollout require the robots to have the same morphology?

The proposal specifies same-motion/different-effect rollouts, but it does not further specify a morphology condition for that kind of rollout. The cross-morphology condition is explicit for the different-motion/same-effect rollouts. I would keep that distinction rather than adding an unstated restriction.
And “cross-morphology” belongs specifically to the different-motion/same-effect comparison?

Yes. That comparison uses rollouts across robot morphologies where the motions differ but the effect is the same. It is the part of the proposal that directly connects the training contrasts to transfer across different robot bodies.
What should the verb embeddings become invariant to?

The aim is for them to be morphology-invariant: the representation of a verb should not depend on one robot body or one characteristic movement when different bodies can achieve the same effect. That does not mean erasing distinctions between different effects. The same-motion/different-effect contrast is there precisely to preserve those distinctions.
Could “morphology-invariant” be misread as ignoring everything a robot actually does?

It could, but that is not what the proposal says. The rollouts still involve motions and effects. The intended invariance is to differences in morphology that should not change the relevant verb grounding when the instructed effect is the same, not to evidence about whether an effect occurs.
How does this connect to goal-conditioned control rather than only to recognizing verbs?

The proposed verb embeddings are for goal-conditioned control. In other words, the learned grounding is meant to help control behavior in relation to an intended goal, not merely assign a word to a movement after observing it. The proposal does not specify a controller design or claim a control result.
If two motions look alike but their effects differ, what pressure is the training supposed to create?

Conceptually, that contrast should discourage EffectBind from treating visual or kinematic similarity of motion as sufficient evidence of the same action meaning. The differing effects must remain distinguishable in the learned grounding, even though the motions match.
What is the corresponding pressure from the cross-morphology rollouts?

They should discourage EffectBind from requiring a particular motion pattern for a verb. If different motions across morphologies achieve the same effect, the embeddings should capture what those rollouts share in relation to the instructed effect rather than treating their movement differences as decisive.
Is the proposal to make all movements across morphologies equivalent?

No. It calls for recognizing different motions as connected when they achieve the same effect, while distinguishing effects that differ even when the motions are the same. Morphology-invariant verb embeddings are not indiscriminate motion-invariant embeddings.
I want to be careful about what a rollout contributes here. Do we need to specify an exact format?

No exact format is stated. A rollout serves as an instance in which motion and effect can be compared. The proposal identifies the two contrasts to use for training EffectBind, but it does not prescribe the rollout format, how effects are recorded, or how examples are collected.
Could I describe one contrast as preventing a false match and the other as preventing a false mismatch?

As a conceptual explanation, yes. Same-motion/different-effect rollouts guard against treating matching motions as a match in effect. Cross-morphology different-motion/same-effect rollouts guard against treating different movements as a mismatch when their effects match. Those are explanations of the proposed contrasts, not reported outcomes.
Does the proposal say that an embedding should encode a complete description of the robot?

No. It proposes morphology-invariant verb embeddings for goal-conditioned control. That describes the desired relationship between the verb representation and differences in robot morphology; it does not specify the embedding’s contents, dimensionality, or how robot-specific information is represented elsewhere.
What would be lost if I shortened the proposal to “train on cross-morphology rollouts”?

That would leave out both the contrastive structure and the specific opposing comparisons. The proposal is not simply to include multiple morphologies. It calls for same-motion/different-effect rollouts as well as cross-morphology different-motion/same-effect rollouts, so that EffectBind learns to separate effects when motions match and relate effects when motions differ.
And if I shortened it to “learn morphology-invariant verbs,” would that also be incomplete?

Yes. That names the desired property but omits how the proposal seeks it: training EffectBind contrastively on those two kinds of rollout. It also omits that the resulting verb embeddings are intended for goal-conditioned control.
Can you give me a concise version that retains every part of the proposal?

Propose training EffectBind on contrastive same-motion/different-effect rollouts and cross-morphology different-motion/same-effect rollouts, with the aim of learning morphology-invariant verb embeddings for goal-conditioned control.
So we should call those the intended training contrasts, without implying they have already produced a transferable model?
Exactly. They are the proposed training contrasts and the stated aim. The proposal does not report completed training, measured transfer, or a demonstrated control outcome.
On unseen grippers, can EffectBind distinguish sliding from rotation when identical wrist trajectories actuate prismatic versus revolute joints?

That is the open question. The wrist trajectories are identical, but the joints they actuate differ: a prismatic joint permits sliding motion, whereas a revolute joint permits rotation. EffectBind would need to distinguish the resulting action rather than assign the same interpretation solely because the wrist followed the same path. The question does not establish that it can already do so.
Why specify the wrist trajectory as identical?

It removes a convenient motion cue for telling the cases apart. If the wrist paths differed, a distinction between sliding and rotation might follow from those paths alone. Here, the same wrist trajectory accompanies different joint motion, so the distinction cannot rest simply on recognizing the wrist path.
Am I asking whether EffectBind recognizes the gripper type?

Not just that. The question is whether, on unseen grippers, EffectBind can distinguish sliding from rotation under this particular contrast: identical wrist trajectories actuating prismatic versus revolute joints. Identifying a gripper’s form would not, by itself, answer whether the resulting action is distinguished.
Could you explain the joint terms without adding a specific setup?

A prismatic joint moves by translation along a permitted direction; a revolute joint moves by rotation about an axis. In this question, that distinction is what makes sliding and rotation possible outcomes of identical wrist trajectories. No particular gripper design, object, or trajectory shape is specified.
Does “identical wrist trajectories” mean the resulting joint motions are identical too?

No. The question deliberately separates them. The wrist follows an identical trajectory in both cases, while the actuation concerns different joint types. The point is to ask whether EffectBind can distinguish the sliding associated with the prismatic joint from the rotation associated with the revolute joint despite that shared wrist motion.
And the grippers must be unseen?

Yes. “On unseen grippers” is an essential condition of the question. It asks about distinguishing these actions when the grippers are not ones EffectBind has seen before, not merely about recognizing a familiar gripper’s response to a familiar wrist trajectory.
What would a motion-only interpretation get wrong here?

If it treated the wrist trajectory as the whole action, it could give the two cases the same interpretation because that trajectory is identical. The question asks whether EffectBind instead retains the difference between sliding and rotation when the same wrist movement actuates different kinds of joint.
Is the distinction about what the wrist intended to do, or about what happened at the joint?

The contrast in this question is between sliding and rotation at the actuated joints, despite identical wrist trajectories. It does not specify a separate instruction or a particular intention for each case. It asks whether EffectBind can distinguish the resulting kinds of action rather than collapsing them into the shared wrist movement.
Would saying “same movement, different action” be precise enough?

It captures the intuition, but it leaves out what is held constant and what changes. More precisely: the wrist trajectories are identical, while actuation of prismatic versus revolute joints gives rise to the sliding-versus-rotation distinction. The question asks whether EffectBind can make that distinction on unseen grippers.
Does the question imply that every wrist trajectory will actuate both kinds of joint?
No. It poses a specific condition in which identical wrist trajectories actuate prismatic versus revolute joints. It does not make a general claim about every trajectory or every gripper.
Could EffectBind answer correctly just by learning that one named joint type means sliding and the other means rotation?

That would capture the conceptual distinction between the joint types, but the question is about EffectBind distinguishing the actions on unseen grippers under identical wrist trajectories. It does not say what information EffectBind is given about a joint’s type or how it would make the distinction, so we cannot assume a particular route to an answer.
I want to avoid turning this into a claim that EffectBind handles unseen grippers.

Then keep it interrogative: can EffectBind distinguish sliding from rotation on unseen grippers in this condition? Neither the question nor the proposed training approach supplies a result. A positive answer would need to be established; it is not part of the stated question.
How does this question relate to the two training contrasts we discussed?

It is a focused instance of the same-motion/different-effect issue that motivates the EffectBind proposal. Holding the wrist trajectory identical makes it especially important not to equate the observed wrist motion with the resulting sliding or rotation. The question asks whether that intended distinction carries over to unseen grippers; it does not report that the proposed training has achieved it.
Is cross-morphology transfer still relevant even though this question names grippers specifically?

Yes, through the condition that the grippers are unseen. The question focuses the broader transfer concern on grippers with prismatic versus revolute joints. It does not, however, specify any wider collection of morphologies or ask for a general transfer result beyond this sliding-versus-rotation distinction.
What if someone describes the cases only as “identical motions producing different effects”?

That gives the general pattern but loses the defining details of this question. The identical motions here are wrist trajectories; the distinction is sliding versus rotation; the trajectories actuate prismatic versus revolute joints; and the grippers are unseen. Keeping those details makes the question precise.
Should I say that the wrist rotates in the revolute-joint case?

Not on the basis of this question. It says the wrist trajectories are identical and that they actuate different joint types. Rotation refers to the revolute joint’s motion, not necessarily to a difference in the wrist’s own trajectory.
So there are two levels of motion that should not be conflated?

Right. There is the shared wrist trajectory, and there is the motion at the actuated joint. The question hinges on their not being interchangeable: the same wrist trajectory can accompany sliding at a prismatic joint or rotation at a revolute joint under the stated condition.
Can the question be answered from the training proposal alone?

No. The proposal describes a way to train EffectBind to attend to differences that motion alone can obscure. This question asks whether EffectBind actually makes a particular distinction on unseen grippers. The proposal motivates the question but does not settle it.
What would count, conceptually, as confusing the two cases?

Treating the prismatic-joint case as rotation, the revolute-joint case as sliding, or treating both as indistinguishable solely because the wrist trajectories match would fail to preserve the stated distinction. The question leaves open whether EffectBind avoids those confusions.
Could we end with the question in its most specific form?
On unseen grippers, can EffectBind distinguish sliding from rotation when identical wrist trajectories actuate prismatic versus revolute joints?
For the unseen-gripper question, what is the specific hypothesis?

The hypothesis is that EffectBind will reach ≥80% slide-versus-rotate accuracy on unseen grippers when wrist trajectories are identical but the outcomes are prismatic versus revolute. That is a predicted level of accuracy under those conditions, not a reported result.
Does “≥80%” include exactly 80%?
Yes. The threshold is at least 80%, so exactly 80% would meet it. The hypothesis does not claim any particular accuracy above that threshold.
I want to make clear what the accuracy is about.

It is slide-versus-rotate accuracy: how accurately EffectBind distinguishes those two outcomes. The hypothesis does not state an instruction-success rate or a general accuracy figure for every action verb.
What makes the identical wrist trajectories important to this prediction?

They hold the wrist-level motion constant across the contrast. If EffectBind reaches the hypothesized accuracy, the distinction between sliding and rotation could not be attributed simply to different wrist trajectories in those cases.
What changes if the wrist trajectory does not?

The stated outcomes differ: one is prismatic and the other revolute. The hypothesis concerns distinguishing sliding from rotation despite the identical wrist trajectories associated with those differing outcomes.
Could I call that “the same motion produces two different outcomes”?

You can use that as shorthand if you specify that the motion held the same is the wrist trajectory. The hypothesis does not say every aspect of motion is identical: sliding and rotation are themselves different outcomes.
Is the prediction about familiar grippers too?
Its specified condition is unseen grippers. It does not make a separate prediction about familiar grippers, so I would keep “unseen grippers” in the statement rather than broadening it.
Does the hypothesis say EffectBind has already distinguished the two outcomes?
No. “Will reach” makes this a hypothesis about expected performance. The ≥80% figure is the predicted threshold, not an observed measurement.
What would reaching that threshold mean in the narrow sense of the hypothesis?

It would mean EffectBind attained at least 80% accuracy at distinguishing slide versus rotate on unseen grippers in cases with identical wrist trajectories but prismatic versus revolute outcomes. By itself, that statement would not specify how EffectBind made the distinction.
And if it distinguished them sometimes, but with less than 80% accuracy?

That would be below the hypothesized threshold. The hypothesis predicts ≥80% slide-versus-rotate accuracy, not merely some ability to distinguish the outcomes. We are not asserting that either result has occurred.
Should I describe the outcome as a prismatic joint versus a revolute joint, or as sliding versus rotation?

The hypothesis uses both parts of that contrast: it predicts slide-versus-rotate accuracy where the outcomes are prismatic versus revolute. Keeping both makes clear what EffectBind is expected to distinguish and what differentiates the outcomes despite the shared wrist trajectory.
I do not want to imply that the wrist itself has to rotate in one case.

Then say that the wrist trajectories are identical, while the outcomes are prismatic versus revolute. Rotation is part of the revolute outcome in the contrast; the hypothesis does not require a different wrist trajectory or say that the wrist itself rotates in only one case.
How directly does this hypothesis address the question about unseen grippers?

It gives that question a specific predicted answer: EffectBind will distinguish sliding from rotation with ≥80% accuracy under the stated unseen-gripper and identical-wrist-trajectory conditions. It remains a hypothesis until there is a result to compare with the prediction.
Can the percentage be stated without the conditions, once the context is established?

For clarity, it is better to keep the conditions attached. “≥80% accuracy” alone could be mistaken for accuracy on other grippers or other distinctions. Here it refers specifically to slide versus rotate on unseen grippers with identical wrist trajectories but prismatic versus revolute outcomes.
Does the hypothesis require perfect separation of sliding and rotation?
No. It predicts an accuracy threshold of at least 80%, not 100%. The important point is the specified level of slide-versus-rotate distinction under the shared-wrist-trajectory condition.
Can we infer from the hypothesis that EffectBind knows which joint is present?

No. The hypothesis predicts accuracy at distinguishing the outcomes; it does not specify what information EffectBind uses or what internal knowledge it has about the joints. Inferring a particular mechanism would go beyond the statement.
Nor does it claim EffectBind can control the grippers successfully, correct?

Correct. This hypothesis is about slide-versus-rotate accuracy, not a control-success measure. It should not be restated as a claim that EffectBind has performed an instruction or controlled an unseen gripper successfully.
What is the shortest version that still says everything essential?
EffectBind is hypothesized to reach ≥80% slide-versus-rotate accuracy on unseen grippers with identical wrist trajectories but prismatic versus revolute outcomes.
And the careful reading is that it predicts an effect-sensitive distinction even though the wrist motion looks the same?

Yes. The prediction is that EffectBind distinguishes the sliding and rotation outcomes at the stated accuracy despite identical wrist trajectories. That interpretation preserves both the contrast and its status as a hypothesis.
What is the concrete plan for investigating whether EffectBind distinguishes sliding from rotation on unseen grippers?

Construct JointSwitch matched-trajectory prismatic/revolute pairs, train EffectBind on six grippers, and measure slide/rotate accuracy on two held-out grippers. The matched-trajectory pairs focus the comparison on different joint outcomes rather than different trajectories. This is a plan, not a report of completed construction, training, or measurement.
What does the name JointSwitch refer to in that plan?
JointSwitch names the planned set of matched-trajectory prismatic/revolute pairs. The name does not, by itself, specify how the pairs are generated or what form their records take.
When you say “matched-trajectory,” what is being held alike?

The trajectories are matched across the prismatic and revolute sides of a pair. In the sliding-versus-rotation question, the shared motion of interest is the wrist trajectory. The plan does not specify a matching algorithm or any further trajectory details.
Why pair prismatic and revolute cases instead of discussing them separately?

Pairing them makes the contrast explicit: a matched trajectory is associated with a prismatic outcome in one case and a revolute outcome in the other. That creates a direct way to examine whether EffectBind distinguishes sliding from rotation when the shared trajectory alone does not distinguish the cases.
Does “matched” mean the prismatic and revolute outcomes should also look the same?
No. It refers to the trajectories being matched, not to making the outcomes identical. The different prismatic and revolute outcomes are the distinction the plan is designed to examine.
What is the training part, exactly?

Train EffectBind on six grippers. The plan identifies that training set size and the JointSwitch paired contrast, but does not specify a training schedule, model configuration, or the number of pairs.
And the measurement is on grippers outside those six?
Yes. Slide/rotate accuracy is to be measured on two held-out grippers, meaning those grippers are not among the six used for training. Keeping that separation is part of the stated plan.
Should I call the two held-out grippers “unseen”?

In relation to training on the six grippers, yes: they are held out rather than included in that training set. The plan’s specific wording is “two held-out grippers,” which is worth retaining when describing the measurement.
What does the accuracy measure distinguish?

It measures slide/rotate accuracy on the two held-out grippers. The relevant distinction is between sliding associated with the prismatic case and rotation associated with the revolute case under the matched-trajectory comparison.
Could the plan be summarized as just a held-out-gripper test?

That would omit what makes the test focused. The plan first constructs JointSwitch matched-trajectory prismatic/revolute pairs, then trains EffectBind on six grippers, and measures slide/rotate accuracy on two held-out grippers. Both the paired contrast and the held-out measurement matter.
Why is matching the trajectories useful for the question we are asking?

It keeps the comparison from depending on an obvious difference in those trajectories. If the cases are paired by trajectory, a slide-versus-rotate distinction cannot be described simply as noticing that one member of the pair followed a different trajectory. The plan does not say what result that comparison will produce.
Does the plan require a particular way of constructing the JointSwitch pairs?

No particular construction procedure is stated. It commits to constructing matched-trajectory prismatic/revolute pairs under the name JointSwitch, without specifying the apparatus, how matching is verified, or how many pairs there will be.
Are the six training grippers and two held-out grippers interchangeable roles?

Not as the plan is worded. EffectBind is to be trained on six grippers, while slide/rotate accuracy is to be measured on two held-out grippers. The plan assigns those distinct roles; it does not describe an alternative assignment or repeated splits.
Should I say that JointSwitch itself reaches a certain accuracy?

No. JointSwitch names the paired cases to be constructed. Accuracy is the planned measurement of EffectBind’s slide/rotate distinction on the two held-out grippers, and the plan does not report an accuracy value.
Could we describe this as checking whether EffectBind merely follows the shared wrist motion?

Yes, as an explanation of what the comparison probes. With matched wrist trajectories across prismatic and revolute cases, treating that shared motion as the entire answer would obscure the slide-versus-rotate distinction. Measuring accuracy on held-out grippers asks whether EffectBind makes the distinction there; it does not presume that it will.
Does the plan say how EffectBind will make its slide/rotate decision?

No. It states what will be constructed, where EffectBind will be trained, and where slide/rotate accuracy will be measured. It does not specify which signals EffectBind uses to distinguish the outcomes or what internal representation it will rely on.
What if I say the plan measures general instruction success on the held-out grippers?

That would change the stated measurement. The plan specifies slide/rotate accuracy on two held-out grippers, not general instruction success. Keeping the measure narrow preserves what this particular plan is set up to assess.
Does “two held-out grippers” tell us how many examples are evaluated?
No. It tells us the number of held-out grippers, not the number of paired cases or individual observations used to calculate accuracy. Those quantities are not specified in the plan.
Likewise, does “six grippers” tell us the number of training rollouts?
No. Six is the number of grippers used for training EffectBind. The plan does not give a rollout count or state how many JointSwitch pairs each gripper contributes.
Can you state the plan in one sentence without implying any of it has happened yet?
The plan is to construct JointSwitch matched-trajectory prismatic/revolute pairs, train EffectBind on six grippers, and measure its slide/rotate accuracy on two held-out grippers.
What is the distinction between the paired contrast and the held-out condition?

The paired contrast specifies what is compared: prismatic versus revolute outcomes with matched trajectories. The held-out condition specifies where the slide/rotate measurement occurs: on two grippers outside the six used to train EffectBind. They address different parts of the same planned investigation.
So none of the wording should imply that an accuracy figure is already available?
Correct. “Measure slide/rotate accuracy” describes a planned measurement. No accuracy value or completed result is given in this plan.
What is the activity for evaluating EffectBind on the JointSwitch distinction?

Train EffectBind on six JointSwitch grippers, then score its slide-versus-rotate accuracy on matched-trajectory prismatic/revolute trials from two held-out grippers. This specifies the training and scoring activity; it does not report an accuracy result.
Which grippers contribute to training, and which contribute to scoring?

The six JointSwitch grippers are used to train EffectBind. The matched-trajectory prismatic/revolute trials used to score slide-versus-rotate accuracy come from two held-out grippers. Those two are not part of the six training grippers.
Why does the activity say “six JointSwitch grippers” rather than just “six grippers”?

It identifies the training grippers as part of the JointSwitch activity. The stated quantity remains six grippers; it does not tell us how many training trials each contributes or describe their individual designs.
What exactly is scored on the held-out grippers?

EffectBind’s accuracy at distinguishing slide versus rotate is scored on matched-trajectory prismatic/revolute trials from the two held-out grippers. The scored quantity is that distinction, not an unspecified measure of overall performance.
Why retain the matched-trajectory condition when describing the scoring trials?

Because it is central to what the score probes. The prismatic and revolute trials are compared with trajectories matched, so the slide-versus-rotate distinction cannot be reduced to noticing a difference in those trajectories. Saying only “prismatic/revolute trials” would leave out that condition.
Does matching the trajectories make the prismatic and revolute outcomes identical?

No. The trajectories are matched; the outcomes being distinguished remain prismatic versus revolute, corresponding to the slide-versus-rotate distinction. Matching one aspect of the trials does not erase the difference the accuracy score concerns.
Is the scoring performed on trials from all eight grippers?

That is not the stated activity. EffectBind is trained on six JointSwitch grippers, and slide-versus-rotate accuracy is scored on matched-trajectory prismatic/revolute trials from two held-out grippers. The activity does not specify a score across all eight.
Does the activity say how many matched trials come from each held-out gripper?
No. It specifies two held-out grippers and the kind of trials used for scoring, but not a trial count per gripper or a total number of scoring trials.
Can we tell whether the scoring is reported separately for each held-out gripper?

No reporting breakdown is specified. The activity says to score slide-versus-rotate accuracy on trials from two held-out grippers; it does not say whether the scores are combined or reported separately.
How does this activity bear on the prediction of ≥80% accuracy?

It provides a way to obtain the slide-versus-rotate accuracy relevant to that prediction: train on the six JointSwitch grippers and score on matched-trajectory prismatic/revolute trials from the two held-out grippers. The activity supplies no score, so it does not establish whether the ≥80% threshold is reached.
Should I say the activity confirms that EffectBind can tell sliding from rotation?
No. Scoring accuracy is the activity used to assess that distinction. Without the resulting score, the activity alone does not confirm how well EffectBind distinguishes the two outcomes.
If I refer to identical wrist trajectories, am I still describing the same question?

Yes, that is the question motivating the matched-trajectory contrast: whether sliding and rotation can be distinguished when wrist trajectories are identical despite prismatic versus revolute outcomes. For this activity, the precise stated scoring condition is matched-trajectory prismatic/revolute trials from the two held-out grippers.
What does “held-out” protect the distinction from, conceptually?

It means the scored grippers are separate from the six used for training, so the score addresses the slide-versus-rotate distinction on grippers outside that training set. The activity does not specify any broader generalization claim or a result from the held-out trials.
Would it be accurate to say EffectBind is trained on the held-out trials and then scored on them?
No. That would remove the stated separation. EffectBind is trained on six JointSwitch grippers; the scoring trials come from two held-out grippers.
Does this activity tell us the training objective or how EffectBind produces a slide-versus-rotate answer?

No. It names the model, the six training grippers, the two held-out grippers, and the matched-trajectory prismatic/revolute scoring trials. It does not specify an objective, a decision procedure, or the information used to produce an answer.
Could we call the resulting number instruction-success accuracy?
That would change the measure. The activity calls for slide-versus-rotate accuracy on the specified trials. It does not say to score whether a broader instruction was successfully carried out.
